passages.title: On Letters
passages.text: It is tempting to see the decline of handwritten letters as a simple loss. Yet letters were never merely vessels of affection; they were also instruments of control, used to issue orders, settle debts and, occasionally, to deceive. What we mourn, perhaps, is not the letter itself but the slowness it imposed — a slowness that forced writers to weigh their words. Digital messages need not be careless, but their speed makes carelessness easy.

passages.title: The Cartographer's Dilemma
passages.text: When the Royal Society commissioned a new map of the kingdom, it expected precision. What it received was something more troubling. The cartographer, a meticulous woman named Orla Venn, had walked every road herself and discovered that several villages shown on the old maps no longer existed, while others had grown into towns that appeared nowhere. Worse, three 'rivers' turned out to be dry ditches, drawn decades earlier to strengthen land claims. Venn's map was accurate, but it was also politically explosive: it undermined the boundaries on which several noble estates depended. The Society shelved it for a generation. Her story is a reminder that maps are never merely descriptive; they are arguments about who owns the world.

passages.title: In Praise of Boredom
passages.text: We have engineered boredom out of our lives. Every queue, commute and pause is now filled by a glowing screen. Yet psychologists increasingly argue that boredom is not a malfunction but a signal: a prompt to seek something more meaningful. In one study, participants who had first completed a dull task, copying numbers from a phone directory, went on to generate more creative uses for a plastic cup than those who had not. The researchers do not claim that tedium is pleasant, only that it may be productive. The difficulty is that the payoff comes later, while the discomfort is immediate, and a phone offers instant relief.

passages.title: The Octopus Who Escaped
passages.text: Inky, a common New Zealand octopus, had lived contentedly at the National Aquarium for two years when, one night, he staged what staff later called 'the great escape'. Having squeezed through a small gap left at the top of his tank, he slid across the floor and slipped down a fifty-metre drainpipe that led straight to the sea. Keepers were not entirely surprised: octopuses are notorious escape artists, capable of unscrewing jar lids and, in some aquariums, of switching off lights they find irritating by squirting water at them. Rather than replacing Inky, the aquarium decided to celebrate him, and visitor numbers rose sharply in the months that followed.

passages.title: In Praise of Boredom
passages.text: We tend to treat boredom as a problem to be solved, usually by reaching for a screen. Yet a growing body of research suggests that boredom may be quietly useful. In one well-known study, participants who first spent fifteen minutes copying numbers from a phone book came up with markedly more creative uses for a pair of plastic cups than those who went straight to the task. Psychologists believe that when the mind has nothing to engage it, it begins to wander, making unexpected connections. This is not to say that endless boredom is healthy; rather, the occasional empty afternoon may be worth protecting.

passages.title: The Girl Who Taught a Village to Code
passages.text: When the only computer at her school in rural Kenya broke down, twelve-year-old Wanjiru refused to let the coding club die. Instead, she taught her classmates programming logic using cardboard 'robots', pebbles and chalk grids drawn in the playground. Her unplugged lessons proved so popular that younger children began turning up after school, and eventually parents asked to join too. When a charity later donated ten laptops, the teachers found that Wanjiru's students picked up real programming languages far faster than expected. 'They already understood how to think like a computer,' one teacher remarked. 'All they lacked was the machine.'

passages.title: Ask the Editor: Are Book Reviews by Kids Worth Reading?
passages.text: Dear Editor, my class has started writing book reviews for our school website, but my older brother says nobody cares what an eleven-year-old thinks. Is he right? — Leo | Dear Leo, your brother couldn't be more mistaken. Publishers increasingly seek out young reviewers precisely because adults are notoriously poor at predicting what children will love. A good review, whatever the writer's age, does three things: it explains what the book is about without spoiling the ending, it gives honest reasons for the reviewer's opinion, and it helps readers decide whether the book is for them. Keep writing, and you might be surprised who's reading.

passages.title: The Mystery of the Singing Sands
passages.text: In a handful of deserts around the world, sand dunes produce a deep humming sound, sometimes loud enough to be heard ten kilometres away. Marco Polo described the noise in the thirteenth century, attributing it to desert spirits. Scientists have long argued over the real cause. The current consensus is that the sound occurs when dry grains of a particular size avalanche down a slope in unison, their collisions synchronising like the members of a choir. Curiously, the note each dune 'sings' depends not on the dune's size but on the size of its grains, which is why sand from the same dune hums the same note even in a laboratory.

notes.the sound is very beautiful: Beauty isn't the point of the comparison.

questions.q: What determines the note a dune produces?

passages.title: A Letter from the Head of the Robotics Team
passages.text: Dear parents, I am delighted to report that our robot, Sparky, finished third out of forty teams at the regional championships. This is all the more remarkable given that, two days before the event, a software update wiped most of the team's code. Rather than panicking, the students divided the work, rewrote the essential functions overnight and stripped out every feature that wasn't strictly necessary. Ironically, the judges praised Sparky's 'elegant simplicity'. We now qualify for the national finals in March, for which we will need help with transport and, as ever, snacks.
